title: Experiment Design and Statistical Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain experiment Design and Statistical Testing and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in experiment Design and Statistical Testing to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study experiment Design and Statistical Testing within Model Evaluation, Validation, and Reliability. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Evaluation is part of system design, not an afterthought. A metric is useful only when it reflects the goal, data conditions, and error costs.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: An experiment defines a hypothesis, outcome, comparison, sample plan, and analysis before interpreting results. Statistical significance, effect size, uncertainty, and practical importance are related but distinct.

items.title: Confidence intervals
items.text: A confidence interval communicates sampling uncertainty under a specified statistical procedure and its assumptions. It is not a guarantee that an individual prediction is correct or that a particular interval has a fixed probability after observing it.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what experiment design and statistical testing takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: An experiment defines a hypothesis, outcome, comparison, sample plan, and analysis before interpreting results. Statistical significance, effect size, uncertainty, and practical importance are related but distinct. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: build a tiny synthetic dataset for experiment design and statistical testing, establish a simple baseline, and define a suitable metric before looking at results. Separate development decisions from final evaluation and describe one important error.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
